label: paragraph_title
text: CANTON BATTLE.

label: text
text: (Continued from Page 1, J. J.

label: text
text: Meanwhile active war is break-ing out in other parts of the province.

label: text
text: General Fan Shok-sang, erstwhile, the strong man of Canton, is reported to be withdrawing his troops, from the upper reaches of the West River and a statement has been made that he has declared neutrality. His non-participation will mean a big difference to the Cantonese cause.

label: text
text: Field telephones have enabled the Yunnanese to maintain communication with exposed stations on the "Canton-Kowloon Railway and a little transport can be moved along a short part of the Canton-Shiukwan Railway up the North River.

label: text
text: Allies of the Reds are reported to be concentrating at Suimshui junction where they will combine with the Cantonese detachment from Kongmoon district, now murching to their colleagues' aid. This fore interests to take Fatshan as a jumping-off point for an onslaught on the west of Canton. If history is repeated, Shameen will be in close proximity to the firing zone. The Yunnanese are shortening their line of defence to the west of Canton and have made Wongsha, the district adjacent to the western suburb, their main line of defence against the Red attack from the West River. No news has come in from the North River.

label: text
text: General Hsu Shung-chi is moving an offensive on Canton by land and sea. His land expedition, numbering about 10,000 layonets, has taken Pingshan with little resistance as the Yunninese fell back on Shektan. General Cheung Kai-shek has dispatched reinforcements in the shape of 2,000 or so eadiets, (in reality actual regular soldiers, but under Russian officers), to the main camp at Whampoa, the naval station below Canton. Another 5,000 of the Cantonese troops are awaiting embarkation for Whampoa.

label: text
text:
The Yunnanese headquarters predict that Hsu will make for the middle of the Canton-Kowloon Railway and march up the line. The Whampoo force, they expect will strike at a part of the railway nearer Canton and thus try to break the Yunnanese main force in the east. Once the two Red branches join hands, they will make a combined assault on Canton. However, the mercenaries declare they are prepared and have their counter-moves.
Accordingly, the Yunnanese are

label: text
text: Accordingly, the Yunnanese are now banging away at Honam with the object of threatening Whampou, if possible.

label: text
text: No sally across the river from either side has been reported. To-morrow, I am told, the Yunnanese will make an attempt on Honam and heavy fighting is expected with a wider range of possibilities. To date, neither side has secured any military advantage since war actually broke out on Saturday. The mrechants in the city are bearing up well.

label: paragraph_title

THIEF JUMPS INTO THE
HARBOUR

label: text
text: At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning," a Chinese youth was sentenced to three months' hard labour for stealing a quantity of lead solder from the Kowloon Docks on Saturday.

label: text
text: It transpired in evidence that on being intercepted by a watchman, the accused jumped into the harbour with the object of swimming to the opposite shore, but was obliged to come back.

label: paragraph_title
text: BITES BY DOGS.

label: text
text: Three cases of attacks by dogs were reported to the Police yesterday, the victims in each case being given medical treatment and the animals being sent to Kennedy Town for observation.

label: text
text: At Kowloon, a dog belonging to Mr. M. A. Johnson, of 10 Chatham Road, bit a Chinese living at 5 Torres Building.

label: text
text: Another dog attacked a Chinese in Queen's Road East near the military quarters.

label: text
text: A servant boy was bitten by a white mongrel owned by Mr. L. Gutierrez, of 39 Bonham Road.

label: paragraph_title
text: LASH FOR THIEF.

label: text
text: SNATCHEID HANDBAG.

label: text
text: EN OFINO BATTERY RATE

label: text
text: The smatching of a hand bag from a European lady at Battery Path had its sequel at the Central Magistracy this morning before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest, when a Chinese youth was charged with the offence. The accused pleaded not guilty.

label: text
text: The complainant, Miss W. Riddle, a nurse at Victoria Hospital, the Peak, slated in evidence that she was walking along buttery Euth at $30 p.m. yesterday when the accused slatched her purse from her hand and ran away. She gave chase as far as the Cathedral Hall. At this point a European boy and Mr. J. M. Shroff kept behind the accused, who ran in the direction of the Government buildings. The purse was loind on the roadside with some of the silver money shrewn on the ground. A sum of about $6 in silver and notes was missing.

label: text
text: Evidence was also given by Mr. Shroff and an Indian consulate. The former stated that he saw the accused running away with the purse in his hand and complainnt following behind. Witness joined in the chase. Near the new P.W.D. building the accused was tripped by in European boy. Pickling himself up and discarding the purse, the accused got behind the building and slid down the drain pipe into Battery Pitch. Witness shouted to an Indian constable on duty at the junction below to arrest the runaway, but the latter evaded the Indian by jumping over the railing into Queen's Road. The accused was later caught by a European.

label: text
text: Sub-Inspector Spour stated that Mr. C. Bowick, of Messrs. Dobwell and Co., Edd, was responsible for the arrest. On being searched at the charge room in the Sub-Inspector's presence the accused had on him $10 in notes, two keys, a police whistle and a pawn ticket. After a statement made by the accused in which he denied the charge, his Worship said that the evidence was quite clear and imposed in sentence of four months' hard labour and life strokes of the birth.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, Mr. A. Duncan was charged with reckless driving of a motor cycle at Nathan Road on May 25.

label: text
text: The defendant informed His Worship that the Police had made a mistake in charging him instead of his brother.

label: text

label: paragraph_title
text: $5,000 BAIL FORFEIT.

label: text
text: MOTOR CAR ACCIDENT SEQUEL

label: text
text: Ball of $5,000 was estreated at the Central Magistracy this morning in the case in which Pun Pul-sang was charged with manslaughter. The case arose out of the motor accident at Pokfulam Road last week when the accused, who was said to have had no licence to drive a car, was alleged to have run on to the pavement and killed a sleeping coolie. Another coolie was seriously injured and is still in hospital. The accused did not put in an appearance and is believed to have absconded.

label: text
text: ACCUSED MAN MISSING.

label: text
text: Pun Luk-chi, the licensed driver of the car, who was alleged to have been seated beside his brother, Pun Pui-sang, at the time of the accident, was charged with unlawfully allowing another man to drive the car. A fine of $100 was imposed.

label: paragraph_title
text: WRONG TURN.

label: text
text: MOTOR CYCLIST FINEO

label: text
text: Before Mr. E. W. Hamilton, at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, Mr. F. Munn, a motor cyclist, appeared for the second time recently for a breach of traffic regulations by taking a wrong turning at Hunghom.

label: text
text: After the evidence of a traffic officer, the Magistrate said that the defendant would do well to make himself conversant with the traffic regulations as soon as possible and imposed a fine of $5.

label: text
text: To a remark from the defendant that he understood there was another charge pending against him, the Magistrate said that there were no reductions for taking a quantity, but the effect would rather be the contrary.

label: paragraph_title
text: FRENCH BANK

label: text
text: EFFECT BEING GIVEN TO AGREEMENT.

label: text
text: In accordance with the interest they have in the Banque Industrielle de Chine creditors will have issued to them in August bonds which will be redeemable by yearly drawing or repurchase.

label: text
text: It will be remembered that in an interview the maringer of the Bank which has taken over the affairs of the Bank Industrielle explained shortly after the announcement of the scheme of settlement that the bonds would be secured on the Boxer indemnity which in itself was secured by the Chinese Maritime Customs and the Salt Tax. "The bonds will be the same as any other bonds," he said, "and the owners will be able to discount them anywhere."

label: text
text: Money for the dividend which is due in July has been deposited by the Chinese Maritime Customs and the warrant for this will be attached to the bonds when issued.

label: paragraph_title
text: BABY'S LIFE.

label: text
text: CRIPPLED PORTER ON FOOTBOARD.

label: text
text: The prompt action of a young railway porter, Bert Lucas, turned what might have been a domestic tragedy into a comedy at Victoria's Station (South-Eastern Section).

label: text
text: Just before the 8.3 p.m. train to Gillingham left No. 4 platform a woman with a girl, aged 12, and another child, aged 1, had been saying good-bye to relatives leaving by the train. The woman had left her baby in the carriage when the train suddenly started.

label: text
text: Her elder daughter's screamed out: "Grandfather is taking away the baby," and as the train gathered speed the woman in the compartment held the baby out of the carriage window over the platform.

label: text
text: Lucas, thinking that the frantic woman was about to drop the baby from the moving train, ran the length of two carriages, sprang upon the footboard, and worked his way along towards the compartment. He seized the baby from the woman, and, although he is a cripple, having been injured in a shunting accident, regained the platform without losing his balance or dropping the child.

label: text
text: The mother by this time was in a fainting condition, and Lucas held the child until she was restored. He refused to accept any reward, and, without waiting for the thanks of the family, said that he was only doing his duty and walked away.

SNAKE SWALLOWS LIVE

label: text
text: CAUSILWAY DAY INCIDENT.

label: text
text: A snake over twelve feet long, and several inches in diameter was not by a Chinese police officer at a hiking village, near Causeway on Sunday evening.

label: text
text: It is believed that the snake was driven from its home by the recent heat and rain. The story goes that it was in the process of swallowing a cat, whole, when the animal's series drew the policeman's attention. The fired five shots at the reptile with his revolver, two of which lodged in the snake's neck and caused its death.

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: A message from Fez states that French warships seized two German trawlers in Morroccan waters near Agadir and took them to Mogador where they have been detained.

label: text
text: OUTFLANKED.

label: text
text: A bulletin from Fez reports that contingents of rebel tribesmen proceeding in the direction of the Taunat heights were outflanked by French cavalry and friendly tribesman and forced to retreat with heavy losses. The French artillery stopped a fresh enemy attack.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text:
Curious stories of the practice of the occult sciences wore told when the libel-nation brought by Liout-Colonel William Joseph Roskell, of New Cavendish Street, W., against Arthur Ady, of Penton-place, Konnington, was continued.
Mr. Ady, who admits the libel, contended that the words were true and fair comment on Col. Roskell's conduct is proprietor of the Delphie Club, for those interested in spiritualism, in Regent Street.
One of the alleged libels was that Col. Roskell added and abetted notorious women in obtaining money from the public by fortune telling.

label: text
text: NEW THOUGHT MOVEMENT: Col. Roskell denied that he had permitted fortune-telling in the club.

label: text
text: Questioned about some of the people who had been mentioned in the libels, Col. Roskell said a Mr. Hall Simpson had lectured on the new though movement.

label: text
text:
Mr. Justice Sunkey: What is the new thought movement?—I believe it is the sort of idea that if you think right you get everything right. If you want something you have to think it right and you get it.
Col' Roskel agreed that symbolic dancing and astral dealing were also subjects of lectures.

label: text
text: Mr. Justice Snukey: What is stroll dealing?—I imagine it is that they now call Conemm. It is nothing to do with the stars.

label: text
text: Mr. Melville (for Mr. Ady): Did you call it the Delphi Club to recall the oracle of Delphi in pre-Christian days when people went to the priest so as to be able to get information about what might happen to them in the future?—It seemed a suitable name.

label: text
text: With regard to Mrs. Susann Harris, Col. Roskell said that Mr. Ady himself had told him that she was not a fortune teller because she used a trumpet, which made it a mechanical experiment. He had never heard that at one demonstration, Mr. Ady put his foot upon the trumpet, closing it up, but "the voices" kept on coming, and it turned out to be Mrs. Harris herself speaking all the time.

label: text
text: Col. Roskell admitted that he allowed Mrs. Bush to come to the club, although he knew she was a convicted swindler. That was viewed as a martyrdom. He agreed that palmistry was practised at the club.

label: text

label: text

label: text
text: Further cross-examined, Col. Roskell said a lecture was given on "Angels, Their Origin and Work." It was also a custom at the club to have a "ghost evening" just about Christmas time. The members would sit around the fireside and relate the most unusual ghostly experiences that had occurred to them.

label: text
text: Re-examined, Col. Roskell said the members of the club were middle-class people of respectable character.

label: text
text: Mr. Hawke, K.C., (for Col. Roskell), remarked that he saw some of the members were people of title.

label: text
text: Detective-Inspector Albert Kirchner, of New Scotland Yard, said as far as could be ascertained Mr. Ady's real name was Jack Breslau Taylor. He claimed to be an American. When he (the detective) arrested Mr. Ady a large number of libels concerning Col. Roskell were found.

label: text
text: Under the Aliens Act Mr. Ady had been recommended for deportation.

label: text
text: Since serving a term of imprisonment he had been on parole. The American authorities had been unable to establish his identity. Advised he was born in a ship in the Red Sea.

Mr. Justice Sunkey, in summing up, described the libel as one of the most atrocious it was possible to imagine. "I do not think you will think I am using too strong an expression when I say that the defendant is a blackguard," he said.
Without retiring, the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff and gave him £200 damages.
